article.overview: Sample collection system is a payload class covering the hardware used to acquire lunar regolith and rock samples and to package them for transfer. It includes the hand tools and drive tubes used by Apollo astronauts, the automated drills and scoops of uncrewed Soviet and Chinese sample-return missions, and the sealed containers that limit contamination of the returned material. No single design defines the category: Apollo relied on crew-operated tools, Luna missions used an automated drill feeding a return capsule, and Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 used robotic sampling with sealed containers. The name describes a function, not one instrument, so mass, dimensions and performance must always be tied to a named system and source.
article.description: A sample collection system acquires material from the surface or subsurface, transfers it into a container and keeps it isolated until laboratory analysis. In its simplest form it is a scoop, a pair of tongs or a rake operated by an astronaut, and tubular core or drive tools pushed or hammered into the regolith to recover layered soil [1][4]. In automated missions a robotic arm or drill performs the same function, supported by cameras and a mechanism that deposits the material into a container [5][6]. Sealing is central to the design, because the sample must be isolated from contamination between collection and analysis [3]. The category therefore combines mechanical sampling, sample handling and containment engineering.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a sample collection system is to obtain material whose composition and structure can be studied in laboratories on Earth. The Smithsonian's record for an Apollo Special Environmental Sample Container states that its purpose was to isolate samples from possible contamination during transfer, and that its contents could be analysed on Earth for uncontaminated details of chemical composition [3]. Apollo drive tubes recovered layered regolith to depths of roughly 30 to 70 cm [4]. Automated missions extended sample return beyond the crewed sites: Luna 24 is reported to have sampled as deep as two metres [2], and Chang'e 6 returned far-side material [5]. Applications include mineralogical and geochemical analysis of returned material. The specific scientific investigations depend on each mission's sample programme and are not documented for every system described here.
article.operating_principle: Sampling methods differ by mission generation. Apollo astronauts used hand tools, including scoops, tongs and rakes for surface material, and core or drive tubes for subsurface material [1]. The Apollo 11 and 12 drive tubes had an inner diameter of about 2 cm and a Teflon-sleeved liner, whereas the Apollo 15 to 17 tubes were thin-walled stainless steel with an inner diameter of about 4.1 cm [4]. The uncrewed Soviet Luna missions used an automatic drill at the end of a sampling arm, which moved the material into a spherical return container [2]. The Chang'e 5 drill is reported in an abstract to have penetrated 1 m into the regolith and collected 259.72 g of drilled sample [7]. The Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 surface systems use cameras to guide the samplers, deposit the material into a sealed container and hand the container to the ascent vehicle [6][9]. Where sealed containers are described, sealing is the step that protects the sample during transfer and return [3][6].
article.scientific_importance: Sample collection determines which material ultimately reaches laboratories, so the design of a sampling system sets the limits of later analysis. Apollo sample containers were designed to isolate samples from contamination during transfer [3]. Automated systems extended sample return beyond the crewed landing sites: the Smithsonian summary gives returned sample masses of about 101 g for Luna 16, 55 g for Luna 20 and 170.1 g for Luna 24 [2]. Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 demonstrated modern robotic sampling and sealed packaging, and the Chang'e 6 mission is reported to have returned about 1.9 kg of far-side samples [5]. The lesson from these missions is that sampling and sealing methods strongly influence the quality and quantity of returned material, but no single historical example defines a standard for future systems.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a sample collection system. The examples below describe specific historical or recent hardware. Values are given as stated by the cited sources, and where a source gives no value this is recorded as not stated. Tool counts, tube diameters and sample masses are not directly comparable between designs that used different sampling principles.

examples.name: Apollo drive tubes and core tubes (crewed, Apollo 11–17)
examples.mass_kg: Individual drive tubes about 0.05 kg to about 2 kg across the 21-tube set; per-type mass not stated
examples.inner_diameter_cm: Apollo 11 and 12 about 2; Apollo 15 to 17 about 4.1
examples.summary: Crew-operated sampling tools on Apollo 11 to 17 are tabulated in NASA's geology tools list [1]. Core tubes were carried on Apollo 11 (2), 12 (4) and 14 (6), while Apollo 15, 16 and 17 carried lower and upper drive tubes, a lunar surface drill and core stems [1]. A third-party sample compendium reports 21 shallow drive tubes across six Apollo missions, penetrating about 30 to 70 cm, with individual tube masses from about 50 g to about 2 kg across the set [4]. The Apollo 11 and 12 tubes had an anodised aluminium outer barrel and a two-part inner barrel with a Teflon sleeve, and an inner diameter of about 2 cm [4]. The Apollo 15 to 17 tubes were thin-walled stainless steel with an inner diameter of about 4.1 cm and a length of about 34 cm, sized to fit the lunar sample return container [4]. The NASA tool list gives counts only and does not give tube dimensions [1], so the compendium's dimensions are not independently confirmed here.

examples.name: Apollo Special Environmental Sample Container
examples.summary: The Smithsonian object record describes a Special Environmental Sample Container of the Apollo programme, manufactured by Union Carbide, Nuclear Division, from 304L stainless steel [3]. The record lists its dimensions as 12.7 cm by 6.7 cm, without stating which dimensions these are [3]. Its open end had a knife edge, and the lid had an indium/silver seal, both covered by a Teflon sheet until the astronauts closed the can [3]. The record describes this as the larger of two container types, states that the type flew on each of the six successful lunar missions, and notes that the use of this specific can is undocumented. Its mass is not stated [3].

examples.name: Soviet Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 automated sample return
examples.type: Historical uncrewed lunar sampling and return systems
examples.sampled_depth: Luna 16 a few tens of centimetres (summary); Luna 24 up to two metres (summary); Luna 20 not stated
examples.summary: Luna 16 (1970) collected soil with an automatic drill at the end of its sampling arm. The arm moved the soil into a spherical, ablative return sample container placed on top of the vehicle, which then returned to Earth [2]. The Smithsonian summary describes the sampled depth as a few tens of centimetres (about a foot) and the sample as 101 g [2]. Luna 20 (1972) is described as very similar in design and sampling method, with a sample of 55 g [2]. Luna 24 (1976) sampled as deep as two metres and returned 170.1 g in total [2]. The summary notes a rerun after technical difficulties with Luna 23's drilling arm, but it does not describe Luna 24's drill type or how its sample was sealed [2].

examples.name: Chang'e 5 robotic drill and surface sampling system (2020)
examples.summary: Chang'e 5 (2020) used a robotic drill and a robotic surface sampler. A 2023 International Journal of Robotics Research article, known from its abstract, reports a 2-metre-class robotic drill that penetrated 1 m into the lunar regolith and collected 259.72 g of sample on 2 December 2020 [7]. The full article could not be retrieved, so these figures rest on the abstract alone. The surface sampling hardware is reported as Sampler A, Sampler B, near-field cameras and a sealing and packaging system, built by the Hong Kong Polytechnic University; a robotic arm lifted the sealed container into the ascender [9]. Other summaries give a total returned mass of 1,731 g [8]. The sources read do not establish how the drilled and scooped masses combine into this total.

examples.name: Chang'e 6 Surface Sampling and Packing System (2024)
examples.type: Recent uncrewed lunar sampling and sealed packaging system
examples.summary: A Hong Kong Polytechnic University news item dated 7 June 2024 describes the Chang'e 6 Surface Sampling and Packing System, developed with the China Academy of Space Technology. The system has two samplers, Sampler A and Sampler B, which PolyU designed and manufactured, and two high-temperature near-field cameras that guide sampling, deposition, container pick-up and insertion into the ascender [6]. The sealing and packaging system comprises a sample container and a sealing device that closes the container after sampling [6]. The news item gives no mass, dimensions, capacity, temperature rating or sample quantity for the samplers or the container [6]. A peer-reviewed paper in Light: Advanced Manufacturing describes a vision-based method in which a binocular point cloud supports terrain analysis and sample-point selection, using a scooping sampler on a four-degree-of-freedom arm; ten sample points were selected for the plan, and the average scooping-depth error after fine-tuning was 3.8 mm in Earth testing-ground trials [5]. The paper reports a returned sample of 1.9 kg and does not describe the container-sealing mechanism [5].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Apollo 11 and 12 drive tubes had an inner diameter of about 2 cm, and Apollo 15 to 17 tubes had an inner diameter of about 4.1 cm and a length of about 34 cm [4]. The Apollo Special Environmental Sample Container is listed at 12.7 cm by 6.7 cm [3]. Dimensions of the Luna, Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 sampling hardware are not stated in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Individual Apollo drive tubes weighed from about 50 g to about 2 kg across the 21-tube set, with per-type values not stated [4]. The mass of the Apollo sample container is not stated [3]. Sampler and container masses for Chang'e 6 are not stated [6]. Returned sample masses are given in the examples above.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources read for any example. The Apollo tools were manually operated, and the Luna, Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 systems must have had power supplies, but no values were found.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A sample collection system must work in the lunar surface environment and must keep collected material isolated during transfer and return. After sealing, the Apollo Special Environmental Sample Container's contents, including a near-vacuum sample of the lunar atmosphere, could be analysed on Earth [3]. The Chang'e 6 cameras are described as high-temperature types, but no temperature rating is given [6]. A Chang'e 5 robotic drill abstract reports terrestrial tests under atmospheric and vacuum conditions [7]. Thermal, radiation, dust and surface-loading requirements for the specific hardware described here are not stated in the sources read, so they are not specified in this article.
article.limitations: A sample collection system's performance is limited by how deep it can reach, how much material it can collect, the mass allowed for the sampler and its container, the risk of contamination and the reliability of the sealing. Crew-operated tools depend on astronaut time and mobility. Automated systems depend on vision, control and mechanism reliability, and the Smithsonian summary notes technical difficulties with Luna 23's drilling arm [2]. The Apollo drive-tube dimensions and the Chang'e 5 drill figures are drawn from a third-party compendium and from an abstract respectively, rather than from primary mission reports [4][7].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Sample collection hardware is carried to the Moon as part of a crewed or robotic mission. For crewed Apollo missions, tools were used by astronauts on the surface, with a tool carrier flown on Apollo 15 and 16 [1]. Automated sample-return systems carried their sampling hardware on the lander or ascent chain, and the sample container was transferred to the return vehicle [2][6].
transportation_process: Integrate the sampling hardware, sample containers and any drill or drive-tube assemblies into the mission hardware on Earth. For Apollo, NASA's tool list shows the number of each tool and sample container carried on each mission [1].
Launch and transfer the hardware to the Moon, and transport it to the lunar surface, either carried by astronauts in the crewed Apollo missions [1] or as part of an automated lander [2][6].
Collect material using hand tools and drive tubes (Apollo), an automatic drill (Luna) or robotic samplers with cameras (Chang'e 5 and 6) [2][5][6][9].
Deposit the material into a container and seal it, where sealing is described [3][6].

Transfer the sealed container to the return chain. Some Apollo 15 to 17 drive tubes were capped on the Moon and returned in vacuum containers, and one container was reported to have leaked to about half an atmosphere [4]. Luna material went into a return capsule on top of the vehicle [2], and the Chang'e 6 sampler placed the container into the ascender [6].
Power, data and thermal interfaces are not specified in the sources read for these examples.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo astronauts used hand tools and pushed or hammered drive tubes into the regolith [1][4]. The Luna sampling was automated with a drill on a sampling arm [2]. The Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6 systems used robotic arms with near-field cameras [6][9]. The sources do not give mounting, levelling or thermal interfaces for these systems.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 11 to 17, Luna 16, Luna 20, Luna 24, Chang'e 5 (2020) and Chang'e 6 (2024) provide historical examples of the sampling hardware described above [1][2][4][5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover, spacecraft or future mission is asserted. The Chang'e 6 sampler's insertion of the container into the ascender [6] describes that mission's architecture only and is not a verified interface specification for any other vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo programme collected lunar samples with hand tools and drive tubes across six landing missions, and the Special Environmental Sample Container type flew on each of the six successful lunar missions [1][3][4]. Soviet automated sample return showed that a robotic drill and a sealed return capsule could return lunar soil without a crew: Luna 16 (1970), Luna 20 (1972) and Luna 24 (1976) [2]. Chang'e 5 (2020) and Chang'e 6 (2024) extended this to vision-guided robotic sampling and sealed packaging, and Chang'e 6 returned far-side material [5][6][9].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name 'sample collection system' describes a function rather than a standard design, so the Apollo tools, Luna drills, Chang'e 5 drill and scoop and Chang'e 6 samplers are not interchangeable. Values such as mass, dimensions, depth and sample quantity must always be tied to the named hardware and source. Several figures come from secondary or summary sources: the Apollo drive-tube dimensions and tube weights come from a third-party compendium [4]; the Chang'e 5 drill figures come from an abstract whose full text could not be retrieved (HTTP 403) [7]; the Chang'e 5 total sample mass of 1,731 g comes from an encyclopaedia summary [8]; and the Chang'e 5 hardware architecture comes from a PolyU summary that was not opened in full [9]. The Chang'e 5 drill depth should also be checked against primary CNSA or peer-reviewed publications. Several specifications are not publicly stated in the sources read: sampler and container masses and dimensions for Chang'e 5 and Chang'e 6, the Chang'e 6 container temperature rating, sample container capacity, power consumption, and the sealing mechanisms of the Luna and Chang'e 5 containers. No direct image asset URLs were verified in this run.

data_quality_notes: No direct image asset URLs were verified within this run's research budget. The image registry and all section-level image arrays are empty; image research is an open item.
The Chang'e 5 Robotics paper (DOI 10.1177/02783649231187918) was read only as a search-result abstract; the publisher page returned HTTP 403.
Chang'e 5 drill penetration is 1 m in the abstract. Other summaries suggest a deeper drill; this discrepancy is unresolved and should be checked against primary CNSA or peer-reviewed sources.
Luna 20 sample mass is 55 g in the Smithsonian summary. Some summaries give 30 g; this was not used.
Luna 16 sampled depth is described as a few tens of centimetres in the Smithsonian summary. A search summary gave 35 cm; this was not used.
Chang'e 6 returned mass is 1.9 kg per the Light: Advanced Manufacturing body text. A search summary gave 1,935.3 g; this was not used as a primary value.
A search summary gave a Chang'e 6 container mass of about 360 g from PolyU-affiliated material. It was not verified on a primary page and is excluded.
The Apollo Special Environmental Sample Container record lists 12.7 cm by 6.7 cm without stating which dimensions these are, and gives no mass.
The Apollo drive-tube dimensions and tube weights come from a third-party compendium (Apollo in Real Time), not from an official NASA technical document.
